The Gospel of ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ is the first half of a two-part work. Both volumes are addressed to the same man, ⟦p:theophilus_2849|Theophilus⟧, and both are the work of ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧. He appears by name only three times, all in ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s letters. Paul calls him the beloved physician, counts him among his fellow workers, and, writing from prison near the end of his life, says that only Luke is with him. In several stretches of Acts the narrative shifts quietly from they to we, as the writer joins Paul on the road. Paul lists him apart from his Jewish fellow workers, for Luke was a Gentile, the only Gentile writer in the New Testament.

⟦p:theophilus_2849|Theophilus⟧ himself stays in the background. The name means friend of God. Luke tells him plainly what he has set out to do. Many others have already written accounts of these events. Luke has gone over everything from the beginning, drawing on those who were eyewitnesses from the start, so that he can write an orderly account, and Theophilus can be sure of what he has been taught. Luke does not claim to have been there himself. He belongs to the next generation, and he has done his research. Much of what he tells is shared with ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧, but a large part of his material appears nowhere else.

⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ sets his story firmly in the Roman world. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧'s story begins and ends in that temple. It opens with an elderly priest burning incense in the sanctuary and closes with the disciples there, praising God. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has been baptised in the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, and the voice from heaven has called him beloved Son. Now, full of the Holy Spirit, he is led into the wilderness for forty days, and there ⟦p:satan_2476|the devil⟧ comes to him with three temptations. Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ returns to ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ in the power of ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, and news of him spreads through the whole region, as far as ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧ and back. 5:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has been preaching from synagogue to synagogue, and the crowds are growing. Now he is standing by the Lake of ⟦l:gennesaret_458|Gennesaret⟧, ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧'s name for the Sea of ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, and the people are pressing so close that he climbs into a fishing boat to speak to them. What happens after the teaching changes Simon's life, and the lives of his partners ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, the sons of ⟦p:zebedee_2998|Zebedee⟧.

In one of the towns a man covered with leprosy, cut off from ordinary life by his disease, falls on his face before ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. One day, as Jesus teaches, the Pharisees appear for the first time in ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧, a movement of devout laymen known for their strict keeping of the law, sitting with teachers of the law among people gathered from every village of ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. The criticism that began at ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧'s banquet now sharpens. Two Sabbath incidents follow one another. ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ opens this chapter with a glimpse of how ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' travelling company is made up and supported. With the Twelve go a number of women who have been healed, among them ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧ called Magdalene, after Magdala, a town on the western shore of the lake, and Joanna, whose husband manages ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s household. The Galilean ministry is reaching its height, and before this chapter is over ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ will have turned his face toward ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.

First he sends the Twelve out on their own to preach and heal. 10:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is now on the road to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and the chapter opens with a wider mission than the one in chapter nine. The journey continues, and ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ shows ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ at prayer once again. 12:
The confrontation at the Pharisee's table is barely over when a crowd of many thousands gathers, so large that people are trampling one another. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks first to his disciples, and much of this chapter is his teaching to them, with the crowd listening in.

13:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still teaching on the road when some in the crowd bring him news: Galileans killed by ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧ while they were offering their sacrifices. Jesus adds a second recent disaster, eighteen people killed when a tower collapsed at ⟦l:siloam_1096|Siloam⟧ in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and uses both to call his hearers to repentance. 14:
For the third time in ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧'s gospel, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is a guest at a Pharisee's table. This time it is the home of a leading Pharisee, on a Sabbath, and the other guests are watching him closely. In front of him is a man suffering from dropsy, a painful swelling of the body, and the old question of healing on the Sabbath is raised once more, this time by Jesus himself.

The first half of the chapter is table talk. Dinners in that world were carefully graded occasions, and the seat a guest took showed his rank. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ watches the guests jostle for the places of honour and has something to say to them, and then something to the host about whom he invites. When another guest makes a pious remark about the feast in the kingdom of God, Jesus answers with a parable about a great banquet and the excuses of those invited.

Then the scene opens out to the road again. Large crowds are travelling with ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, and he turns to them with some of the hardest words in the gospel about what it costs to follow him.
15:
The crowds following ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ now include many tax collectors and others whom respectable people called sinners, and they are drawing close to hear him. The Pharisees and scribes look on and grumble that he welcomes such people and even eats with them. To share a meal was a sign of acceptance, and that is what offends them.

This one complaint is the setting for the whole chapter. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ answers it with three parables, each about something lost and then found, and each ending in celebration. The first two are brief: a shepherd with a hundred sheep and a woman with ten silver coins.

The third, often called the parable of the prodigal son, is the longest and most loved of all the parables in ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧. In the world of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' hearers, a younger son asking for his inheritance while his father was alive would have seemed a deep insult, and a Jew reduced to feeding pigs, unclean animals under the law, could hardly sink lower. But the story does not end with the younger son. It ends with his older brother standing outside, angry, refusing to come in to the celebration, while the grumbling Pharisees and scribes listen.
16:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has just answered the Pharisees with the parables of the lost. Now he turns to his disciples, and the subject becomes money.

The chapter opens with one of the most surprising parables in the gospels, the story of a dishonest manager who is about to lose his position and quickly reduces the debts owed to his master, so that he will have friends when he is out of work. The master commends him for his shrewdness. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ draws out a series of sayings about faithfulness with wealth, ending with the warning that no one can serve both God and money.

⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ tells us the Pharisees loved money, and they scoff. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ answers with a few brief sayings about the law and about divorce, and then with a second story.
